notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Science uses observation, evidence, measurement and experimentation to understand natural phenomena.
  • Scientific evidence can be used to reconstruct past events.
  • Science helps explain present-day processes.
  • Scientific models help estimate possible future conditions.
  • Scientific predictions are based on evidence, patterns and established principles.
  • Scientific prediction is not the same as fortune-telling.
  • New evidence can modify scientific interpretations of the past.
  • Improved instruments increase the accuracy of scientific observations.
  • Interdisciplinary research combines knowledge from different branches of science.
  • Geology, archaeology, palaeontology, astronomy, genetics and climatology are important for reconstructing the past.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Past → Evidence

Present → Observation and Measurement

Future → Models and Prediction

2. Understanding the Past Through Science
  • Direct observation is impossible for many events that occurred in the distant past.
  • Scientists reconstruct past events using evidence that survives in the present.
  • Fossils provide evidence about organisms that lived in the past.
  • Rocks preserve information about Earth's geological history.
  • Archaeological remains provide evidence about past human societies.
  • Ice cores preserve information about ancient atmospheric conditions.
  • Tree rings provide information about past environmental conditions.
  • Sediments can preserve biological and climatic evidence.
  • DNA provides information about biological ancestry and evolutionary relationships.
  • Astronomical observations allow scientists to study the distant past because light takes time to travel.
📌 Remember

Past cannot always be observed directly → Past is reconstructed from evidence.

3. Geology
  • Geology is the scientific study of the Earth, its materials, structure and history.
  • Rocks are important records of Earth's geological past.
  • Sedimentary rocks commonly contain fossils.
  • Rock layers are called strata.
  • The study of rock layers is called stratigraphy.
  • Stratigraphy helps determine the relative ages of geological formations.
  • Lower undisturbed sedimentary layers are generally older than upper layers.
  • This principle is called the law of superposition.
  • Geological evidence helps reconstruct ancient environments.
  • Geological studies help explain earthquakes, volcanoes and plate movements.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Strata → Stratigraphy

Lower layer → Generally older

Upper layer → Generally younger

4. Law of Superposition
  • The law of superposition is used in relative dating.
  • In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rocks, the oldest layer is generally at the bottom.
  • Successively younger layers occur above older layers.
  • The principle was developed during the early history of geology.
  • Nicolas Steno is strongly associated with the principle of superposition.
  • Superposition determines relative age, not exact numerical age.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Relative dating → Older or younger.

Absolute dating → Numerical age.

5. Relative Dating
  • Relative dating determines whether one object or geological layer is older or younger than another.
  • Relative dating does not directly give an age in years.
  • Stratigraphy is an important relative-dating method.
  • Fossils can help correlate rock layers of similar age.
  • Index fossils are particularly useful for relative dating.
  • The law of superposition is a basic principle of relative dating.
6. Absolute Dating
  • Absolute dating estimates the numerical age of an object or geological formation.
  • Radiometric dating is an important absolute-dating technique.
  • Radiometric dating uses the predictable decay of radioactive isotopes.
  • Different radioactive isotopes are suitable for different age ranges.
  • Carbon-14 dating is commonly used for relatively recent organic remains.
  • Very old rocks are commonly dated using isotopes with much longer half-lives.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Relative Dating → Sequence

Absolute Dating → Numerical Age

7. Radioactive Dating
  • Radioactive isotopes decay at characteristic rates.
  • The rate of radioactive decay is expressed using half-life.
  • Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
  • Radioactive decay provides a natural clock for dating materials.
  • Radiometric dating compares parent and daughter isotopes.
  • Radiometric dating is widely used in geology and archaeology.
  • The reliability of radiometric dating depends on appropriate sample selection and assumptions about the system being dated.
8. Carbon-14 Dating
  • Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope of carbon.
  • Carbon-14 dating is also called radiocarbon dating.
  • It is used mainly for dating once-living organic material.
  • Bone, wood, charcoal, cloth and other organic remains may be suitable for radiocarbon dating.
  • Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years.
  • Carbon-14 dating is most useful for archaeological and relatively recent geological materials.
  • It is generally not suitable for dating extremely old rocks millions of years old.
  • Willard Libby developed the radiocarbon dating technique.
  • Willard Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960 for developing radiocarbon dating.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Carbon-14 → Organic remains → 5,730 years → Willard Libby

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Carbon-14 is not the standard method for dating the age of the Earth.

9. Potassium-Argon Dating
  • Potassium-40 is a radioactive isotope used in geological dating.
  • Potassium-40 decays partly to argon-40.
  • Potassium-argon dating is useful for very old rocks.
  • It is particularly useful for dating volcanic rocks.
  • It is commonly used in studies of human evolution when fossils occur near volcanic layers.
  • Potassium-40 has a very long half-life of about 1.25 billion years.
📌 Remember

Carbon-14 → Relatively recent organic remains.

Potassium-Argon → Very old volcanic rocks.

10. Uranium-Lead Dating
  • Uranium-lead dating is one of the oldest radiometric dating techniques.
  • Uranium isotopes decay into stable isotopes of lead.
  • Uranium-lead dating is useful for dating very old rocks.
  • Zircon crystals are especially useful for uranium-lead dating.
  • Zircon can incorporate uranium when it forms while initially excluding much lead.
  • Uranium-lead dating has helped determine the age of ancient rocks and minerals.
11. Age of the Earth
  • Scientific evidence indicates that Earth is approximately 4.54 billion years old.
  • The age of Earth has been estimated mainly using radiometric dating.
  • Meteorites provide important evidence for estimating the age of the Solar System.
  • The oldest terrestrial minerals are zircon crystals.
  • Earth's age cannot be determined using carbon-14 dating.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Age of Earth → About 4.54 billion years

12. Fossils
  • Fossils are preserved remains, impressions or traces of organisms from the geological past.
  • Fossils provide direct evidence of past life.
  • Bones, teeth and shells may become fossils.
  • Footprints and burrows may be preserved as trace fossils.
  • Fossilisation is more likely when remains are rapidly buried.
  • Hard body parts generally fossilise more readily than soft tissues.
  • Fossils are particularly common in sedimentary rocks.
  • Fossils help reconstruct evolutionary history.
  • Fossils help scientists infer ancient environments.
  • The fossil record is incomplete because fossilisation requires special conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fossils → Past Life → Evolution + Ancient Environment

13. Types of Fossils
  • Body fossils preserve parts of an organism's body.
  • Trace fossils preserve evidence of an organism's activity.
  • Footprints are trace fossils.
  • Burrows are trace fossils.
  • Coprolites are fossilised faeces.
  • Petrified fossils form when minerals replace or fill organic tissues.
  • Mould fossils preserve the impression of an organism.
  • Cast fossils form when a mould is later filled with minerals or sediment.
  • Organisms may sometimes be preserved in amber.
📌 Remember

Coprolite → Fossilised faeces

Trace fossil → Activity of organism

14. Palaeontology
  • Palaeontology is the scientific study of ancient life through fossils.
  • A scientist who studies fossils is called a palaeontologist.
  • Palaeontology combines geology and biology.
  • Fossils provide evidence for biological evolution.
  • Palaeontologists reconstruct ancient organisms and ecosystems.
  • Fossil succession helps determine the relative ages of rock formations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Palaeontology → Fossils → Ancient Life

15. Index Fossils
  • Index fossils are fossils useful for correlating and relatively dating rock layers.
  • A good index fossil belonged to an organism that was geographically widespread.
  • A useful index fossil existed for a relatively short geological period.
  • Index fossils help identify rock layers of similar age in different locations.
  • Index fossils are primarily used for relative dating.
16. Evolutionary Evidence
  • Fossils provide historical evidence of changes in organisms over time.
  • Comparative anatomy provides evidence of evolutionary relationships.
  • Homologous structures indicate common evolutionary ancestry.
  • Vestigial structures can provide evidence of evolutionary history.
  • Embryological similarities may indicate shared ancestry.
  • Molecular evidence compares DNA and protein sequences.
  • Genetic similarities are used to reconstruct evolutionary relationships.
  • Biogeography studies the geographical distribution of organisms and provides evidence for evolution.
17. Archaeology
  • Archaeology is the scientific study of past human societies through material remains.
  • Archaeologists study tools, pottery, buildings, burials, inscriptions and other artefacts.
  • An artefact is an object made or modified by humans.
  • Archaeological excavation must carefully record the position and context of discoveries.
  • Stratigraphy is important in archaeology.
  • Radiocarbon dating is widely used for organic archaeological remains.
  • Archaeology combines evidence from geology, chemistry, biology, anthropology and history.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Archaeology → Material remains of human past

Palaeontology → Ancient life through fossils

18. Archaeology and Tamil Nadu
  • Archaeological excavations are important sources for understanding ancient Tamil society.
  • Adichanallur is an important archaeological site in Tamil Nadu.
  • Keezhadi is an important archaeological site in Sivaganga district.
  • Kodumanal is an important archaeological site in Erode district.
  • Porunthal is an archaeological site in Dindigul district.
  • Paiyampalli is an important prehistoric archaeological site in Tamil Nadu.
  • Archaeology provides material evidence that complements literary and inscriptional evidence.
  • Scientific dating methods help establish the chronology of archaeological remains.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Keezhadi → Sivaganga

Kodumanal → Erode

Porunthal → Dindigul

19. Dendrochronology
  • Dendrochronology is the scientific dating of tree rings.
  • Trees generally form growth rings annually in seasonal climates.
  • Ring width can reflect environmental conditions during a growing season.
  • Patterns of tree rings can be matched between different trees.
  • Dendrochronology can provide precise calendar-year dates under suitable conditions.
  • Tree rings can provide information about past droughts and climatic conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dendrochronology → Tree Rings → Past Climate and Dating

20. Ice Cores
  • Ice cores are cylindrical samples drilled from glaciers and ice sheets.
  • Layers of ice accumulate over time.
  • Ice cores can preserve bubbles of ancient atmosphere.
  • Air bubbles allow scientists to measure past concentrations of atmospheric gases.
  • Ice cores provide evidence about past carbon dioxide and methane levels.
  • Stable isotopes in ice can provide information about past temperatures.
  • Dust and volcanic ash preserved in ice cores provide additional environmental evidence.
  • Antarctica and Greenland are major sources of long ice-core climate records.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ice Core → Ancient Atmosphere + Past Climate

21. Sediment Cores
  • Sediments accumulate on lake beds and ocean floors.
  • Sediment cores preserve layers representing different periods.
  • Pollen preserved in sediments can reveal past vegetation.
  • Microfossils can indicate past environmental conditions.
  • Volcanic ash layers can help correlate sediments across regions.
  • Sediment chemistry can provide information about past climate and pollution.
22. Palynology
  • Palynology is the scientific study of pollen and spores.
  • Pollen grains can remain preserved for long periods.
  • Different plant species produce distinctive pollen.
  • Fossil pollen helps reconstruct past vegetation.
  • Changes in vegetation can provide evidence about past climate.
  • Palynology is useful in archaeology, geology and palaeoecology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Palynology → Pollen and Spores

23. Speleothems
  • Speleothems are mineral deposits formed in caves.
  • Stalactites and stalagmites are examples of speleothems.
  • Their chemical and isotopic composition can record past climatic conditions.
  • Cave deposits can sometimes be dated using uranium-series methods.
  • Speleothems are useful palaeoclimate archives.
24. Varves
  • Varves are annual layers of sediment deposited in some lakes.
  • One pair of seasonal layers can represent approximately one year.
  • Varves can be counted to estimate elapsed time.
  • Varve thickness can provide information about past environmental conditions.
25. Historical Climate Reconstruction
  • Past climate is reconstructed using proxy evidence.
  • A climate proxy is an indirect indicator of past climatic conditions.
  • Tree rings are climate proxies.
  • Ice cores are climate proxies.
  • Pollen is a climate proxy.
  • Corals can provide climate information.
  • Sediments can preserve climatic evidence.
  • Multiple independent proxies improve confidence in climate reconstruction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Proxy → Indirect evidence of past climate

26. Corals as Climate Records
  • Corals form growth bands that can preserve environmental information.
  • Coral skeletons contain chemical signals related to seawater conditions.
  • Coral records can provide information about past sea-surface temperatures.
  • Corals are useful for reconstructing tropical ocean conditions.
  • Coral growth can also provide evidence of past sea-level changes.
27. Understanding Human History Through Genetics
  • DNA carries hereditary information.
  • Genetic differences among populations can provide clues about common ancestry.
  • Mitochondrial DNA is inherited mainly through the maternal line.
  • Y-chromosome markers can be used to study paternal lineages.
  • Ancient DNA can be extracted from some preserved biological remains.
  • Ancient DNA helps reconstruct migration, ancestry and relationships among ancient populations.
  • Genetic evidence should be interpreted together with archaeological and historical evidence.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ancient DNA → Ancestry + Migration + Population History

28. Molecular Clock
  • A molecular clock estimates evolutionary divergence using genetic changes accumulated over time.
  • Molecular clocks depend on estimates of mutation rates.
  • Fossil evidence can be used to calibrate molecular clocks.
  • Molecular-clock estimates involve uncertainty.
  • Molecular clocks are useful for reconstructing evolutionary relationships.
29. Study of the Past Through Astronomy
  • Astronomy allows scientists to observe objects as they existed in the past.
  • Light travels at a finite speed.
  • The speed of light in vacuum is approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
  • A light-year is a unit of distance, not time.
  • One light-year is the distance travelled by light in one year.
  • Light from distant stars takes years to reach Earth.
  • When astronomers observe a distant galaxy, they see it as it existed when the observed light began its journey.
  • Observing increasingly distant objects allows astronomers to investigate earlier stages of cosmic history.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Light-year → Unit of distance, not time.

30. Looking Back in Time
  • Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
  • Therefore, the Sun is observed as it was roughly 8 minutes earlier.
  • Light from the nearest stars takes several years to reach Earth.
  • Light from distant galaxies can take millions or billions of years to reach Earth.
  • Astronomy therefore provides direct observational access to earlier stages of the Universe.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Distance in Space → Look-back Time

31. Present-Day Science
  • Present-day phenomena can be studied directly using observation and measurement.
  • Sensors convert physical quantities into detectable signals.
  • Scientific instruments extend the capabilities of human senses.
  • Microscopes reveal structures too small for the naked eye.
  • Telescopes detect distant astronomical objects.
  • Satellites provide large-scale observations of Earth.
  • Computers process large amounts of scientific data.
  • Real-time monitoring is widely used in weather, earthquakes, pollution and health.
32. Scientific Instruments
  • A microscope is used to observe very small objects.
  • A telescope is used to observe distant objects.
  • A thermometer measures temperature.
  • A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
  • A hygrometer measures humidity.
  • An anemometer measures wind speed.
  • A rain gauge measures rainfall.
  • A seismograph or seismometer records seismic waves.
  • A spectrometer analyses properties of light or other spectra.
  • A pH meter measures acidity or alkalinity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Links

Temperature → Thermometer

Pressure → Barometer

Humidity → Hygrometer

Wind speed → Anemometer

Rainfall → Rain Gauge

Earthquake waves → Seismometer

33. Remote Sensing
  • Remote sensing obtains information about an object or area without direct physical contact.
  • Satellites and aircraft are widely used for remote sensing.
  • Remote sensing detects reflected or emitted electromagnetic radiation.
  • Remote sensing is used in agriculture.
  • It is used for forest monitoring.
  • It is used for mapping water resources.
  • It is used for mineral exploration.
  • It is used for disaster assessment.
  • It is used for weather observation.
  • It is used for land-use and land-cover mapping.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Remote Sensing → Observe without physical contact

34. Satellites
  • Artificial satellites orbit Earth or other celestial bodies.
  • Earth-observation satellites collect information about land, oceans and atmosphere.
  • Weather satellites monitor clouds and storms.
  • Communication satellites relay signals over large distances.
  • Navigation satellites help determine position and time.
  • Remote-sensing satellites provide repeated observations of large areas.
  • Satellite imagery allows changes over time to be compared.
35. Indian Remote Sensing
  • India has developed a major Earth-observation and remote-sensing programme.
  • Indian Remote Sensing satellites are commonly referred to as IRS satellites.
  • Remote-sensing data are used in agriculture, forestry, water resources and disaster management.
  • ISRO develops and operates many Indian Earth-observation satellites.
  • Satellite data support cyclone monitoring and weather forecasting.
  • India's space programme has important applications in communication, navigation and resource management.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

ISRO → Satellites + Remote Sensing + Communication + Navigation

36. Geographic Information System
  • GIS stands for Geographic Information System.
  • GIS stores, analyses and displays geographically referenced information.
  • GIS combines maps with digital data.
  • GIS is used in urban planning.
  • GIS is used in disaster management.
  • GIS is used in agriculture and natural-resource management.
  • GIS can combine satellite data with ground-based observations.
  • GIS helps identify spatial patterns and relationships.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

GIS → Spatial Data → Mapping + Analysis

37. GPS
  • GPS stands for Global Positioning System.
  • GPS uses signals from satellites to determine position.
  • GPS can provide latitude, longitude, altitude and time information.
  • GPS is widely used in navigation.
  • GPS was developed by the United States.
  • Satellite navigation requires precise timing.
  • India's regional navigation system is NavIC.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

GPS → Navigation using satellites

NavIC → Indian regional navigation system

38. Weather Forecasting
  • Weather forecasting predicts atmospheric conditions over relatively short periods.
  • Weather forecasts use observations from weather stations, satellites, radar, ships and balloons.
  • Numerical weather prediction uses mathematical models of the atmosphere.
  • Computers process large volumes of atmospheric data.
  • Forecast uncertainty generally increases with forecasting time.
  • Weather forecasts are regularly updated when new observations become available.
  • Doppler weather radar is useful for monitoring rainfall and storms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Weather Forecast → Observation + Satellite + Radar + Computer Model

39. Weather and Climate
  • Weather refers to short-term atmospheric conditions.
  • Climate refers to long-term patterns of weather in a region.
  • Weather can change within hours or days.
  • Climate is generally assessed over long periods.
  • A single day's weather does not establish a climate trend.
  • Climate models simulate interactions among atmosphere, oceans, land and ice.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Weather → Short-term

Climate → Long-term pattern

40. Meteorology
  • Meteorology is the scientific study of the atmosphere and weather.
  • Meteorologists analyse temperature, pressure, humidity, wind and precipitation.
  • Weather balloons collect information from the upper atmosphere.
  • Weather radar detects precipitation.
  • Satellites monitor large-scale weather systems.
  • Atmospheric-pressure differences contribute to wind formation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Meteorology → Weather and Atmosphere

41. Cyclone Prediction
  • Tropical cyclones can be monitored using satellites.
  • Weather radars provide detailed information when cyclones approach land.
  • Computer models predict cyclone tracks.
  • Forecasts estimate cyclone intensity and landfall location.
  • Early warning reduces loss of life by enabling evacuation and preparedness.
  • Cyclone forecasting demonstrates the practical value of scientific prediction.
  • Prediction cannot eliminate a cyclone but can reduce disaster risk.
42. Earthquake Science
  • Earthquakes occur when stored energy is suddenly released in Earth's crust.
  • Seismic waves are produced by earthquakes.
  • Seismometers detect ground motion.
  • The epicentre is the point on Earth's surface directly above the focus.
  • The focus or hypocentre is the location inside Earth where rupture begins.
  • Scientists can identify earthquake-prone regions.
  • The exact time, location and magnitude of a future earthquake generally cannot be reliably predicted far in advance.
  • Earthquake early-warning systems detect seismic waves after an earthquake begins and may provide brief warning before stronger shaking reaches some locations.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Earthquakes can be monitored and hazards assessed.

Exact long-term prediction of individual earthquakes is not currently reliable.

43. Volcano Monitoring
  • Volcanoes can be monitored using seismic activity.
  • Ground deformation can indicate movement of magma.
  • Gas emissions provide information about volcanic activity.
  • Satellite observations can detect heat and deformation.
  • Monitoring improves assessment of eruption risk.
  • Not every change in volcanic activity leads to an eruption.
44. Disaster Management Through Science
  • Hazard maps identify areas vulnerable to natural hazards.
  • Satellite images help assess floods, cyclones, landslides and forest fires.
  • Early-warning systems allow preventive action.
  • GIS helps map affected areas.
  • Remote sensing enables rapid assessment over large regions.
  • Scientific forecasting reduces disaster risk when combined with effective communication and preparedness.
  • Disaster mitigation reduces the potential impact of hazards.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Science + Early Warning + Preparedness → Reduced Disaster Risk

45. Flood Forecasting
  • Flood forecasting uses rainfall, river-level and catchment data.
  • Satellite observations help monitor rainfall and inundation.
  • River gauges measure water level and discharge.
  • Hydrological models help estimate flood risk.
  • Early warnings enable evacuation and reservoir management.
  • Flood forecasts contain uncertainty because rainfall and runoff can change rapidly.
46. Drought Monitoring
  • Drought is a prolonged period of abnormally low water availability.
  • Rainfall records are important for drought monitoring.
  • Soil-moisture observations provide information about agricultural drought.
  • Satellite observations can detect vegetation stress.
  • Reservoir and groundwater levels are important indicators.
  • Climate information supports drought preparedness.
47. Agriculture and Scientific Prediction
  • Weather forecasts assist farmers in planning sowing and harvesting.
  • Soil testing identifies nutrient status.
  • Remote sensing helps monitor crop condition.
  • Satellite data can help estimate cultivated area.
  • Pest forecasting can reduce crop losses.
  • Scientific irrigation planning improves water-use efficiency.
  • Crop models can estimate potential yields under different conditions.
48. Medical Science and the Present
  • Medical diagnosis uses observation, laboratory tests and imaging.
  • Blood tests provide biochemical and cellular information.
  • X-rays are widely used for imaging bones and certain internal structures.
  • Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves.
  • CT stands for Computed Tomography.
  • MRI stands for Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
  • MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radiofrequency signals.
  • ECG records the electrical activity of the heart.
  • EEG records electrical activity of the brain.
  • Scientific diagnosis helps identify disease before treatment decisions are made.
🔗 TNPSC Key Links

Heart electrical activity → ECG

Brain electrical activity → EEG

Ultrasound → High-frequency sound

MRI → Magnetic field + Radio waves

49. Epidemiology
  • Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of health-related conditions in populations.
  • Epidemiologists investigate patterns of disease.
  • Incidence refers to new cases occurring during a specified period.
  • Prevalence refers to all existing cases in a population at a particular time or over a period.
  • Epidemiological data help identify risk factors.
  • Disease surveillance helps detect unusual increases in cases.
  • Mathematical models can help estimate how infectious diseases may spread.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Incidence → New cases

Prevalence → Existing cases

50. Future Prediction in Science
  • Scientific prediction uses known relationships and present data to estimate future outcomes.
  • Predictions are usually conditional rather than absolutely certain.
  • The quality of prediction depends on the quality of data and model.
  • Predictions can be improved as new observations become available.
  • Complex systems often have greater prediction uncertainty.
  • Scientific forecasts commonly provide probabilities rather than guaranteed outcomes.
51. Scientific Models
  • A scientific model is a simplified representation of reality.
  • Physical models represent systems in tangible form.
  • Mathematical models represent relationships using equations.
  • Computer models simulate complex systems.
  • Climate models are computer-based representations of the climate system.
  • Weather models simulate atmospheric processes.
  • Epidemiological models simulate disease transmission.
  • Models are tested by comparing predictions with observations.
  • Every model contains assumptions and limitations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Model → Simplified representation → Prediction + Explanation

52. Computer Simulation
  • Computer simulation imitates the behaviour of a real system using computational models.
  • Simulations are useful when direct experimentation is difficult, expensive or dangerous.
  • Weather forecasting relies heavily on computer simulation.
  • Climate research uses computer simulations.
  • Engineering uses simulation to test designs.
  • Simulations can explore multiple possible future scenarios.
  • Simulation output is only as reliable as the model, assumptions and input data.
53. Scenario
  • A scenario is a possible future condition based on specified assumptions.
  • Scenarios are not necessarily predictions of exactly what will happen.
  • Climate studies use scenarios to explore different future pathways.
  • Planning agencies use scenarios to compare possible outcomes.
  • Changing assumptions can produce different scenario results.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Scenario → Possible future under assumptions.

Prediction → Expected outcome based on evidence/model.

54. Extrapolation
  • Extrapolation estimates values beyond the range of observed data.
  • Extrapolation assumes that an observed relationship continues beyond the measured range.
  • Extrapolation is generally less reliable than interpolation.
  • Unexpected changes can make extrapolation inaccurate.
  • Long-range projections therefore involve greater uncertainty.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Interpolation → Within known data range

Extrapolation → Beyond known data range

55. Interpolation
  • Interpolation estimates an unknown value between known observations.
  • Interpolation generally involves less uncertainty than extrapolation when the underlying pattern is stable.
  • Graphs and numerical methods can be used for interpolation.
  • Interpolation is widely used in scientific data analysis.
56. Trend
  • A trend is a general direction of change in data over time.
  • Trends can be increasing, decreasing or relatively stable.
  • Short-term fluctuations should not automatically be interpreted as long-term trends.
  • A larger time series generally provides a better basis for identifying long-term trends.
  • Scientific analysis distinguishes trends from random variation.
57. Probability in Forecasting
  • Probability expresses the likelihood of an event.
  • Scientific forecasts may be expressed as probabilities.
  • A high probability does not guarantee that an event will occur.
  • A low probability does not mean an event is impossible.
  • Probability helps communicate uncertainty.
  • Risk combines the likelihood of an event with its potential consequences.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Probability ≠ Certainty

58. Artificial Intelligence in Science
  • Artificial intelligence enables computer systems to perform tasks involving pattern recognition and prediction.
  • Machine learning is a branch of artificial intelligence that learns patterns from data.
  • AI can assist in medical-image analysis.
  • AI can help analyse astronomical data.
  • AI can assist weather and climate research.
  • AI can help identify patterns in large scientific datasets.
  • AI predictions depend on the quality and representativeness of training data.
  • AI-generated results require scientific validation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

AI → Pattern Recognition + Prediction

Machine Learning → Learn patterns from data

59. Big Data
  • Big data refers to extremely large and complex datasets.
  • Modern scientific instruments generate large quantities of data.
  • Satellites produce large Earth-observation datasets.
  • Genome sequencing produces large biological datasets.
  • Particle-physics experiments generate enormous amounts of data.
  • Computers and statistical tools are used to identify patterns in big datasets.
  • Large quantity alone does not guarantee high-quality evidence.
60. Genetics and Future Medicine
  • Genetic information can help identify inherited disease risks.
  • DNA sequencing determines the order of nucleotides in DNA.
  • Genomic information can support personalised medicine.
  • Gene therapy aims to treat disease by modifying or supplying genetic material.
  • Genetic screening can identify certain inherited variations.
  • Ethical considerations are important in the use of genetic information.
61. Biotechnology
  • Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or biological processes for practical applications.
  • Fermentation is an ancient form of biotechnology.
  • Recombinant DNA technology enables DNA from different sources to be combined.
  • Genetically modified organisms contain genetic material altered using biotechnology.
  • Biotechnology is used in medicine, agriculture and industry.
  • Vaccines, insulin and certain enzymes can be produced using biotechnology.
  • Biotechnology has major potential but also requires safety and ethical assessment.
62. Nanotechnology
  • Nanotechnology deals with materials and structures at the nanometre scale.
  • One nanometre equals 10⁻⁹ metre.
  • Materials may show different properties at the nanoscale.
  • Nanotechnology has applications in medicine.
  • It has applications in electronics.
  • It has applications in materials science.
  • Nanomaterials require assessment for potential health and environmental effects.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nano → 10⁻⁹ metre

63. Space Science and the Future
  • Space science improves understanding of Earth, the Solar System and the Universe.
  • Space technology supports communication.
  • It supports navigation.
  • It supports weather forecasting.
  • It supports disaster management.
  • It supports resource mapping.
  • Robotic spacecraft can explore environments unsuitable for humans.
  • Space telescopes avoid many limitations caused by Earth's atmosphere.
64. Scientific Prediction vs Astrology
  • Scientific predictions are based on measurable evidence and testable models.
  • Scientific predictions can be checked against later observations.
  • Failed scientific predictions may lead to modification of models.
  • Astrology claims relationships between celestial positions and human events but lacks reliable scientific evidence establishing such causal mechanisms.
  • Astronomy is a natural science studying celestial objects and phenomena.
  • Astrology and astronomy are not the same.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Astronomy → Science

Astrology → Not an established scientific discipline

65. Astronomy vs Astrology
  • Astronomy studies stars, planets, galaxies and other celestial phenomena scientifically.
  • Astronomy uses mathematics, physics and observation.
  • Astrology attempts to associate celestial positions with human affairs.
  • Astronomy produces testable predictions about celestial phenomena.
  • Solar and lunar eclipses can be predicted accurately using astronomy.
  • Planetary positions can be calculated using astronomical models.
66. Prediction of Eclipses
  • A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun.
  • A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon.
  • Orbital motions can be calculated mathematically.
  • Eclipses can therefore be predicted well in advance.
  • Eclipse prediction is an example of successful scientific forecasting based on well-understood physical laws.
67. Renewable Energy and Future Planning
  • Renewable energy comes from sources replenished naturally on human timescales.
  • Solar energy is renewable.
  • Wind energy is renewable.
  • Hydropower is renewable.
  • Biomass is renewable when managed sustainably.
  • Fossil fuels are non-renewable on human timescales.
  • Scientific research improves energy efficiency and storage.
  • Energy forecasting supports planning of future electricity demand.
68. Climate Change Science
  • Climate change is studied using observations, physical principles and models.
  • Instrumental temperature records provide evidence of recent climate change.
  • Ice cores provide information about past climate.
  • Tree rings extend climate records into the past.
  • Satellites provide global observations of the atmosphere, oceans and ice.
  • Climate models explore future conditions under different forcing scenarios.
  • Future climate projections contain uncertainties but are constrained by physical laws and observational evidence.
69. Environmental Monitoring
  • Air-quality monitoring measures pollutants in the atmosphere.
  • Water-quality monitoring measures physical, chemical and biological characteristics.
  • Remote sensing monitors deforestation and land-cover change.
  • Biodiversity surveys track changes in species and ecosystems.
  • Environmental monitoring provides baseline data for future comparison.
  • Long-term observations help identify environmental trends.
70. Science and Sustainable Development
  • Sustainable development seeks to meet present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.
  • Scientific knowledge helps assess resource availability.
  • Science helps measure environmental impacts.
  • Renewable energy technologies support sustainability.
  • Efficient water use supports sustainable development.
  • Conservation science helps protect biodiversity.
  • Scientific evidence supports long-term planning.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Science → Evidence → Sustainable Planning

71. Scientific Uncertainty
  • All scientific measurements have some degree of uncertainty.
  • Uncertainty does not mean a result is unreliable.
  • Uncertainty can often be quantified.
  • Better measurements can reduce uncertainty.
  • Predictions become less certain when projecting further into the future in complex systems.
  • Scientists communicate uncertainty through ranges, probabilities and confidence intervals.
  • Decision-making can still proceed when uncertainty exists.
72. Verification of Predictions
  • A scientific prediction can be tested when the predicted event or observation becomes available.
  • Successful predictions increase confidence in a model.
  • Failed predictions can identify weaknesses in a model.
  • Models may be revised when observations disagree with predictions.
  • Continuous comparison of prediction and observation is an important scientific process.
73. Limitations of Scientific Prediction
  • Science cannot predict every future event with perfect accuracy.
  • Complex systems contain many interacting variables.
  • Incomplete data reduce predictive accuracy.
  • Measurement errors can influence predictions.
  • Model assumptions affect predictions.
  • Random processes can impose fundamental limits on prediction.
  • Scientific forecasts should therefore state their uncertainties.
74. Scientific Knowledge Is Self-Correcting
  • Scientific interpretations are revised when stronger evidence becomes available.
  • Improved dating methods can change archaeological chronologies.
  • New fossils can alter interpretations of evolutionary history.
  • Improved telescopes can reveal previously unknown astronomical phenomena.
  • Better climate records can refine climate reconstructions.
  • Model correction is a normal part of scientific progress.
75. Important Scientists and Links
  • Nicolas Steno → Stratigraphy and law of superposition.
  • Charles Lyell → Uniformitarian geology.
  • James Hutton → Deep time and uniformitarian ideas.
  • Willard Libby → Radiocarbon dating.
  • Charles Darwin → Evolution by natural selection.
  • Alfred Russel Wallace → Natural selection.
  • Edwin Hubble → Expansion of the Universe.
  • C. V. Raman → Raman Effect.
  • Vikram Sarabhai → Indian space programme.
  • Homi J. Bhabha → Indian atomic-energy programme.
76. Uniformitarianism
  • Uniformitarianism holds that natural processes operating today can help explain geological features formed in the past.
  • James Hutton developed important early uniformitarian ideas.
  • Charles Lyell later strongly promoted uniformitarian geology.
  • The phrase “the present is the key to the past” summarises the basic idea.
  • Modern geology recognises both gradual processes and catastrophic events.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Present processes → Help explain past geology

James Hutton + Charles Lyell → Uniformitarianism

77. Deep Time
  • Deep time refers to the immense duration of Earth's geological history.
  • James Hutton contributed significantly to recognition of Earth's great antiquity.
  • Geological processes often operate over millions of years.
  • Radiometric dating later provided numerical evidence for the great age of Earth.
  • Deep time is essential for understanding geological and biological evolution.
78. Must-Memorise Dating Facts
  • Relative dating → Determines older or younger.
  • Absolute dating → Gives numerical age.
  • Stratigraphy → Study of rock layers.
  • Superposition → Lower undisturbed layers are generally older.
  • Nicolas Steno → Superposition.
  • Carbon-14 → Organic remains.
  • Carbon-14 half-life → About 5,730 years.
  • Willard Libby → Radiocarbon dating.
  • Potassium-Argon → Ancient volcanic rocks.
  • Uranium-Lead → Very old rocks and zircon.
  • Dendrochronology → Tree-ring dating.
  • Palynology → Pollen and spores.
  • Ice cores → Ancient atmosphere and climate.
79. Must-Memorise Past–Present–Future Links
  • Fossils → Past life.
  • Archaeology → Past human societies.
  • Stratigraphy → Relative geological age.
  • Radiometric dating → Numerical age.
  • Tree rings → Past climate and dating.
  • Ice cores → Ancient atmosphere.
  • Ancient DNA → Past ancestry.
  • Telescope → Distant Universe and look-back time.
  • Sensors → Present observation.
  • Satellite → Earth monitoring.
  • GIS → Spatial analysis.
  • Weather model → Short-term atmospheric prediction.
  • Climate model → Long-term climate projection.
  • Epidemiological model → Disease-spread estimation.
  • AI → Data-based pattern recognition and prediction.
80. TNPSC Traps
  • A fossil is not necessarily the actual unchanged body of an organism.
  • Fossils are most commonly preserved in sedimentary rocks.
  • Archaeology and palaeontology are not the same.
  • Archaeology mainly studies material remains of human societies.
  • Palaeontology studies ancient life through fossils.
  • Relative dating does not provide an exact age in years.
  • Absolute dating provides a numerical age estimate.
  • Carbon-14 is mainly used for organic remains.
  • Carbon-14 is not suitable for determining Earth's age.
  • Tree-ring dating is called dendrochronology.
  • Pollen study is called palynology.
  • A light-year is a distance.
  • Weather and climate are not the same.
  • Weather is short-term; climate is long-term.
  • Remote sensing does not require physical contact with the target.
  • GIS and GPS are different.
  • GPS determines position; GIS analyses spatial information.
  • Scientific prediction does not mean certainty.
  • Scenario and prediction are not identical.
  • Interpolation works within the observed range.
  • Extrapolation extends beyond the observed range.
  • Exact long-term prediction of individual earthquakes is not currently reliable.
  • Astronomy is a science; astrology is not an established scientific discipline.
  • Scientific models are simplified representations, not perfect copies of reality.
81. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Past → Evidence.
  • Present → Measurement.
  • Future → Prediction.
  • Geology → Earth history.
  • Stratigraphy → Rock layers.
  • Superposition → Lower older.
  • Fossil → Past life.
  • Palaeontology → Fossils.
  • Archaeology → Human past.
  • Radiometric → Radioactive decay.
  • C-14 → Organic remains.
  • C-14 half-life → 5,730 years.
  • Libby → Radiocarbon.
  • Dendrochronology → Tree rings.
  • Palynology → Pollen.

  • Ancient DNA → Ancestry.

  • Remote sensing → No direct contact.
  • GIS → Spatial analysis.
  • GPS → Position.

  • Climate → Long-term.
  • Forecast → Probability.
  • Model → Simplified system.
  • Interpolation → Inside range.
  • Extrapolation → Outside range.
  • AI → Pattern recognition.
  • Nano → 10⁻⁹ metre.
